verdicts.trueWording: an immediately accessible book for anyone with moderate intelligence
verdicts.note: Peter Wright's 'Mapping a Masterwork' (Ultan's Library, 28 Aug 2002), reception paragraph on the paradox of praise, quotes Michael Bishop lauding The Shadow of the Torturer in exactly these words; footnote 2 sources it to Bishop, Thrust, Fall 1980, p.12. Relay chain intact; page continues 'and the ability to read'.

verdicts.trueWording: each basic theory is set forward in a brief essay
verdicts.note: Allbery's eyrie.org review (reviewed 2004-09-12), third paragraph; the sentence continues with the 'some only a few pages' limb, so both limbs of the claim hold.

verdicts.trueWording: without a basic plot synopsis or timeline as a memory refresher
verdicts.note: Same review, the 'two things that bothered me' paragraph; Allbery says without them the reading may be hard going for friends who read New Sun some time back. Fault-finding limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: expects the reader to remember who he's talking about
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: Borski mentions characters, including minor ones, constantly in passing; Allbery particularly missed a dramatis personae. Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I felt a bit stupid to have missed obvious clues
verdicts.note: Fourth paragraph, on the layers Wolfe put into the book. Page hedges with 'In a few places' and 'a bit'; the claim's unqualified 'felt stupid' is a mild flattening, not a break.

verdicts.trueWording: quoted at p.163: is initially a job of decipherment
verdicts.note: Sauve's review relays Clute's sentence verbatim with the page cite [P.163], in the paragraph on the younger Clute's intelligibility. Relay only: Strokes itself not consulted, so the page-163 attribution rests on Sauve.

verdicts.trueWording: the book ends with a substantial series of pieces about Gene Wolfe
verdicts.note: Sauve review, paragraph on Real Year/Real Decade and other meaty critical thoughts; he adds the pieces help in understanding what Wolfe is trying to achieve.

verdicts.trueWording: words that appear to be neologisms but are anything but
verdicts.note: Auerbach, Waggish, 23 Nov 2007, the 'first, there's the style' paragraph; the same sentence supplies the archaism limb ('drawn directly or indirectly from archaic words and usages, often Latin-derived').

verdicts.trueWording: to evoke strangeness while preserving a depth of meaning
verdicts.note: Same style paragraph: the style 'does, however, serve its purpose', and Auerbach gives Wolfe credit for it, so the concessive framing of the claim is accurate.

verdicts.trueWording: What it doesn't do is make the writing beautiful
verdicts.note: Same paragraph, immediately after the strangeness concession; Auerbach calls it one big minus for mainstream acceptance and calls the style clunky.

verdicts.trueWording: Central plot points are skipped over and only referred to in retrospect
verdicts.note: Auerbach's plot paragraph, opening the discussion of elision and narrative unreliability; adjacent sentences add misdirection and points never cleared up.

verdicts.trueWording: destined for public consumption by people in his world
verdicts.note: Paragraph on the stability of the text; the sentence pairs this with Wolfe posing as translator of a manuscript that has travelled long and far.

verdicts.trueWording: we can't derive from the whole what the meaning
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'derive meaning from the parts' inverts the page's direction: Auerbach says the meaning of any particular piece cannot be derived from the whole, not the reverse
verdicts.note: The quoted limb 'we do not have the whole context' is verbatim in the text-stability paragraph, and the missing-context cause is exactly Auerbach's. But the claim reverses part and whole, so the derivation limb as written is not what the page says.

verdicts.trueWording: he reduces the book to decontextualized apocrypha
verdicts.note: Text-stability paragraph, closing sentence; the page's grammatical subject is Wolfe, conditioned on our not grasping Severian's words as more than a maybe-true story, which is the unresolved unreliability the claim names. Page adds the gnostic-gospel figure.

verdicts.trueWording: that Severian is writing for would know and be able
verdicts.note: Comment by MattD, 28 November 2007, on the Waggish post: some element of the truth can be found from what Severian's public would know and could contradict if he lied. Hedged as 'some element', which the claim's 'truth can be recovered' slightly firms up.
